detail:
A systematic review written for the 2017 ACC/AHA/HRS syncope guideline examined 10 studies of pacing for reflex-mediated syncope, six of them in vasovagal syncope. In open-label studies, pacing was associated with about a 70% reduction in recurrent syncope, but the reviewers found limited data supporting pacing beyond a narrower group: people with recurrent vasovagal syncope whose heart rhythm during a spontaneous faint shows a long pause (asystole).

That gap between open-label and blinded results is the central research problem in this area: identifying, before any device is considered, which patients' faints are driven by long pauses. Rhythm documentation during a real episode, for example with an implantable monitor in selected cases, is the evidence path the guideline literature follows.

Tabs is not endorsing or verifying this material. Talk to your doctor or cardiologist about evaluation options for recurrent fainting.
sourceName: Journal of the American College of Cardiology
sourceVideoTitle: Pacing as a treatment for reflex-mediated syncope: a systematic review for the 2017 ACC/AHA/HRS guideline
summary: A systematic review prepared for the 2017 ACC/AHA/HRS syncope guideline found the pacing evidence mixed: open-label studies suggested far fewer recurrences, while blinded trials narrowed any benefit to selected patients with documented long heart pauses.
takeaways: pacing is studied only for selected, frequently fainting patients
blinded trials showed smaller benefits than open-label ones
research focuses on documenting the heart rhythm during a faint
device decisions are specialist decisions; ask your cardiologist
title: Vasovagal syncope research: who benefits from pacing?
